title: Currently doing this challenge called January
content:
I saw this tweet yesterday.

I laughed because, yeah… January has been rough.

We returned from two weeks with family in Colorado and Kansas on January 3. On the morning of January 5, I did a hike with a couple of my fellow hike clubbers. We had decided on the Leacock Memorial Trail in the Pacific Palisades. The views on the hike were some of the most gorgeous, sweeping views of the city. It was a clear day. We could see everything. We were crunched for time and didn’t end up doing the entire loop, but we did make it to Skull Rock and noticed the nearby burn scars from the Lachman Fire, an 8-acre brush fire that happened on New Year’s Day. Two days later, it was where The Palisades Fire apparently started. I haven’t stopped thinking about it.

I finally have a moment to reflect on the level of stress, anxiety and grief I’ve experienced over the last couple of weeks. I remind myself that we are among the lucky ones. We didn’t lose our house. So many others did. We live on the west side of Los Angeles, far enough from The Palisades that we didn’t need to evacuate but close enough that on Tuesday, when the fire was raging and the wind was blowing like I’ve never experienced before, I stayed up through the night listening to the LA Fire Department on the Scanner Radio app. I wasn’t going to wait for an evacuation warning and I wanted to hear firsthand how fast the fire was progressing. There was really no other way to know. While it became apparent that the fire wasn’t going to reach us that night, it was clear that the scale of devastating destruction between the Palisades Fire and the Eaton Fire was unlike anything I had ever seen. It was ferocious and completely out of control. You’ve seen the news, you’ve read the articles, but it’s impossible for a single photo, drone fly-over or single account to capture the magnitude.

Like I said though, we’re among the lucky ones. We know people that have lost damn near everything but their lives. And while I don’t personally know anyone who died in the fires, I know people who lost loved ones. When the exterminator came to the house today, I asked him how he was holding up and if his family was ok. He told us his kid had lost their grandmother in the Eaton Fire. A friend had lost their uncle in the Palisades Fire. Half of a close friend’s daughter’s class and their teachers had ALL lost their homes. The amount of loss is staggering. Unimaginable. But it’s real. The nightmare happened. It is only just becoming apparent. If you think health insurance is hell, imagine dealing with home insurance after this. Or worse, the hell of having lost everything without insurance or your house not burning down, then being caught in the in-between hell of an insurance company who won’t acknowledge that your home is uninhabitable due to the highly toxic smoke and ash that has found its way into everything you own. You can’t afford to buy all new things, can’t find or afford to live in another place and have no time to deal with any of it because you work two jobs. These aren’t hypotheticals.

Los Angeles is my home. I have lived here longer than any other place. My children were born here. I am filled with grief and rage and anxiety and it’s heavy. It crushed me this week. I’ve had more migraines in the last two weeks than I have in the last two years. Last Friday, I even had two in one day. And yet, we are among the lucky ones.

We have air purifiers on full blast in every room of the house. I check three air quality data sets every morning when I wake up and throughout the day. This weekend, I’ll need to do my best to clean the toxic ash off the house and cars, wearing a mask, gloves and protective goggles.

I’ve felt so helpless most of the last two weeks. There have been times of hopelessness, despair and intense sadness. But during one of those times, in a frenzy to do something, I registered lafires.help and put all the resources I had been collecting to help people impacted by the fire on a single web page. Some people eat or go shopping when they’re depressed. I register domains and publish things on the web.

Yesterday, I used an AI to transcribe the two-and-a-half-hour Zoom that the Coalition for Clean Air had this week and then uploaded the transcription to create a custom GPT that was an expert in air quality and cleaning up after a wildfire. This evening, I added the transcript from the public information panel and Q&A that KCRW and R&S Kayne Foundation Los Angeles held this week to the GPT’s knowledge. I’ve asked it a bunch of questions, all of which it has answered thoroughly and taken my stress and anxiety down a few notches. People who have used it have told me it is genuinely helpful, which feels nice. Please let me know if you end up using it.

This week was Cassidy’s twelfth birthday. She was supposed to have a birthday party last weekend, but it became clear that wouldn’t happen. We ended up driving to Joshua Tree to escape the toxic smoke and ash and play on the rocks in Joshua Tree National Park. I felt guilty for leaving throughout the weekend. It was the right thing to do because we could do it, but all I could think about were the people who could not and how deeply they were suffering.

On Thursday, I pitched a problem statement to a class of MBA students at an Ivy League School as part of my new job (that will be a separate post). We lost David Lynch. A new Panda Bear album is coming soon. I got a migraine today during an 8-hour meeting over Zoom. I watched as my daughter’s teacher from her fashion class surprised her (and me) by showing up at our house to gift her a sewing machine. One of my dearest friends is celebrating their birthday. The air may not be great right now, but the sun came up and I can see beautiful blue skies and golden sunshine all along the way. It’s January 18, and we are among the lucky ones.
author: bradbarrish
